person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A REPORTING VOCABULARY WRITTEN IN TWO DAYS BECAUSE THE WORDS DID NOT AGREE - four named categories standing between a chest CT and a diagnosis, with the consequences of each word stated in the same document
span.quote: We propose four categories for reporting CT imaging findings potentially attributable to COVID-19, each with suggested standardized language ( Table 1 ). The reporting language does not offer an exact likelihood for COVID-19 pneumonia, which depends on several factors including prevalence in a community, exposure, risk factors, and clinical presentation. Rather, the reporting language focuses on CT findings reported in the literature and the typicality of these features in COVID-19 pneumonia rather than other diseases. Included in the reporting language are unique coding identifiers in brackets that can then be used for future data mining.

span.label: what language radiologists should use when a chest CT shows findings that could be COVID-19, given that naming the disease sets off a cascade and not naming it may miss it
span.quote: As a result, including “COVID-19” in a radiology report could trigger a cascade of events including infection control measures and anxiety for both the managing provider and the patient.

span.label: THE WORD ITSELF ACTS ON THE PATIENT: `including `COVID-19` in a radiology report COULD TRIGGER A CASCADE OF EVENTS including INFECTION CONTROL MEASURES AND ANXIETY FOR BOTH THE MANAGING PROVIDER AND THE PATIENT`, and `Ordering providers may also feel that having `COVID-19` or `coronavirus` documented in a radiology report CONSTRAINS THEIR CLINICAL DECISION MAKING AND TREATMENT OPTIONS`. The shortest path in this corpus from which word to what happens
span.quote: As a result, including “COVID-19” in a radiology report could trigger a cascade of events including infection control measures and anxiety for both the managing provider and the patient.

span.label: SO A DELIBERATELY BROADER TERM IS RECOMMENDED: `These incidental findings DO NOT NECESSARILY NEED TO BE REPORTED AS COVID-19 PNEUMONIA, with `VIRAL PNEUMONIA` AS A REASONABLE AND INCLUSIVE ALTERNATIVE` - a word chosen for its consequences rather than its precision
span.quote: These incidental findings do not necessarily need to be reported as COVID-19 pneumonia, with “viral pneumonia” as a reasonable and inclusive alternative.

span.label: AND THE COST OF THE BROADER TERM IS NAMED IN THE SAME DOCUMENT: `THE TERM VIRAL PNEUMONIA ENCOMPASSES A RANGE OF IMAGING FINDINGS SOME OF WHICH ARE NOT TYPICAL FOR COVID-19`. Nothing else in this corpus recommends an imprecise term and states the imprecision in the next paragraph
span.quote: It should be noted that viral pneumonias have a wide variety of imaging manifestations, some of which are atypical or less common in COVID-19 such as tree-in-bud opacities and other small nodules, bronchial wall thickening, and bronchial mucus plugs ( 12 ). Thus, the term viral pneumonia encompasses a range of imaging findings some of which are not typical for COVID-19.

span.label: AND THE VOCABULARY REFUSES TO CARRY A PROBABILITY, ON PURPOSE: `The reporting language DOES NOT OFFER AN EXACT LIKELIHOOD for COVID-19 pneumonia, WHICH DEPENDS ON SEVERAL FACTORS including prevalence in a community, exposure, risk factors, and clinical presentation. Rather, the reporting language focuses on ... THE TYPICALITY OF THESE FEATURES`. Four categories that are statements about THE IMAGE and explicitly not about the patient's probability - and they ship with `UNIQUE CODING IDENTIFIERS IN BRACKETS that can then be used for FUTURE DATA MINING`, which is this project's own move made in March 2020 under pressure
span.quote: We propose four categories for reporting CT imaging findings potentially attributable to COVID-19, each with suggested standardized language ( Table 1 ). The reporting language does not offer an exact likelihood for COVID-19 pneumonia, which depends on several factors including prevalence in a community, exposure, risk factors, and clinical presentation. Rather, the reporting language focuses on CT findings reported in the literature and the typicality of these features in COVID-19 pneumonia rather than other diseases. Included in the reporting language are unique coding identifiers in brackets that can then be used for future data mining.

span.label: AND EVERY NUMBER AROUND IT IS A RANGE, FOR THE RIFLE REASON: `The reported sensitivities and specificities of CT for COVID-19 VARY WIDELY (60%-98% AND 25%-53%, respectively) ... likely due to the retrospective nature of the currently published studies, INCLUDING LACK OF STRICT DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR IMAGING and procedural differences for confirming infection`
span.quote: The reported sensitivities and specificities of CT for COVID-19 vary widely (60%–98% and 25%–53%, respectively) ( 26 – 29 ), likely due to the retrospective nature of the currently published studies, including lack of strict diagnostic criteria for imaging and procedural differences for confirming infection.

span.label: THE REFERENCE STANDARD IS ITSELF A RANGE: `Early reports of RT-PCR sensitivity vary considerably, RANGING FROM 42% TO 71%, and an initially negative RT-PCR MAY TAKE UP TO 4 DAYS TO CONVERT in a patient with COVID-19`. The thing the imaging is scored against is between two-fifths and seven-tenths right
span.quote: Early reports of RT-PCR sensitivity vary considerably, ranging from 42% to 71% ( 26 , 27 ), and an initially negative RT-PCR may take up to 4 days to convert in a patient with COVID-19

span.label: AND THE COLLECTION METHOD HALVES THE ANSWER: `in a recently published series of 1070 patients, the majority of samples collected were THROAT SWABS, and THROAT SWABS DETECTED ONLY APPROXIMATELY HALF OF THE POSITIVE CASES THAT WERE DETECTED BY NASAL SWABS`, while `ELEVEN DIFFERENT RT-PCR TESTS were approved for use in China ... WITH VARYING LEVELS OF SENSITIVITY`
span.quote: As an example, in a recently published series of 1070 patients, the majority of samples collected were throat swabs, and throat swabs detected only approximately half of the positive cases that were detected by nasal swabs

span.label: AND A NEGATIVE IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT AND THE TIMING, NOT THE PATIENT: `A SLIGHT MAJORITY OF PATIENTS HAD A NEGATIVE CT DURING THE FIRST 2 DAYS after symptom onset ... Therefore, A NEGATIVE CT SHOULD NOT BE USED TO EXCLUDE THE POSSIBILITY OF COVID-19, particularly early in the disease`
span.quote: A slight majority of patients had a negative CT during the first 2 days after symptom onset with GGO usually developing between day 0 and 4 after symptom onset and peaking at 6–13 days ( 8 , 9 , 22 – 24 ). Therefore, a negative CT should not be used to exclude the possibility of COVID-19, particularly early in the disease.

span.label: AND THE CATEGORY SYSTEM'S OWN COST IS PRINTED: `Reporting `ATYPICAL FEATURES` MAY RESULT IN FALSE-NEGATIVE CASES, and THE RISK OF MISSING COVID-19 CAN HAVE BROAD IMPLICATIONS`
span.quote: Reporting “atypical features” may result in false-negative cases, and the risk of missing COVID-19 can have broad implications.

span.label: AND THE CATEGORIES MEET CASES THEY CANNOT HOLD: `We anticipate cases with MIXED IMAGING FINDINGS, that is, those that have BOTH TYPICAL AND ATYPICAL imaging features ... OVER 20% OF PATIENTS WITH COVID-19 MAY HAVE COEXISTENT INFECTIONS COMPLICATING THE CATEGORIZATION of imaging observations. THE RADIOLOGIST WILL HAVE TO DETERMINE whether or not these findings are part of the same process or are unrelated`
span.quote: We anticipate cases with mixed imaging findings, that is, those that have both typical and atypical imaging features for COVID-19. Recent analysis suggests that over 20% of patients with COVID-19 may have coexistent infections complicating the categorization of imaging observations ( 35 ). The radiologist will have to determine whether or not these findings are part of the same process or are unrelated.

span.label: AND THE VOCABULARY DECLARES ITSELF PROVISIONAL: `Imaging appearances ... are based upon available literature at the time of writing in MARCH 2020, noting the retrospective nature of many reports, including BIASES RELATED TO PATIENT SELECTION ... As radiologists' experience with COVID-19 increases, OUR CATEGORIZATION OF THESE FINDINGS AS TYPICAL, INDETERMINATE, OR ATYPICAL MAY EVOLVE`
span.quote: Imaging appearances in the standardized reporting language are based upon available literature at the time of writing in March 2020, noting the retrospective nature of many reports, including biases related to patient selection in cohort studies, examination timing, and other potential confounders. As radiologists’ experience with COVID-19 increases, our categorization of these findings as typical, indeterminate, or atypical may evolve.

span.label: `typical` - NOT a probability but a statement about the literature: features `REPORTED IN THE LITERATURE TO BE FREQUENTLY AND MORE SPECIFICALLY SEEN IN COVID-19 PNEUMONIA IN THE CURRENT PANDEMIC`. The category is indexed to a moment
span.quote: Typical features are those that are reported in the literature to be frequently and more specifically seen in COVID-19 pneumonia in the current pandemic

span.label: `indeterminate` - features `REPORTED IN COVID-19 PNEUMONIA BUT NOT SPECIFIC ENOUGH TO ARRIVE AT A RELATIVELY CONFIDENT RADIOLOGIC DIAGNOSIS`. A named slot for `the image cannot decide`
span.quote: Indeterminate features are those that have been reported in COVID-19 pneumonia but are not specific enough to arrive at a relatively confident radiologic diagnosis. An example would be diffuse GGO without a clear distribution ( Figs 5 , 6 ). This finding is common in COVID-19 pneumonia but occurs in a wide variety of diseases such as acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Pneumocystis infection, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, which are difficult to distinguish by imaging alone.

span.label: `atypical` - `UNCOMMON OR NOT OCCURRING IN COVID-19 pneumonia AND MORE TYPICAL OF OTHER DISEASES`, and the paper prints a positive-RT-PCR case that falls in it: the category is about the image, not the patient
span.quote: Atypical features are those that are reported to be uncommon or not occurring in COVID-19 pneumonia and are more typical of other diseases such as lobar or segmental consolidation in the setting of a bacterial pneumonia, cavitation from necrotizing pneumonia, and tree-in-bud opacities with centrilobular nodules, as can occur with a variety of community acquired infections and aspiration

span.label: `negative for pneumonia` - `NO PARENCHYMAL ABNORMALITIES THAT COULD BE ATTRIBUTABLE TO INFECTION. Specifically, GGO AND CONSOLIDATION ARE ABSENT` - and immediately: `THERE MAY BE NO FINDINGS ON CT EARLY IN COVID-19`
span.quote: Negative for pneumonia implies that there are no parenchymal abnormalities that could be attributable to infection. Specifically, GGO and consolidation are absent. Importantly, there may be no findings on CT early in COVID-19.

span.label: `viral pneumonia` (as recommended here) - the DELIBERATELY BROADER term, `A REASONABLE AND INCLUSIVE ALTERNATIVE` whose breadth is stated as a cost: it `ENCOMPASSES A RANGE OF IMAGING FINDINGS SOME OF WHICH ARE NOT TYPICAL FOR COVID-19`
span.quote: It should be noted that viral pneumonias have a wide variety of imaging manifestations, some of which are atypical or less common in COVID-19 such as tree-in-bud opacities and other small nodules, bronchial wall thickening, and bronchial mucus plugs ( 12 ). Thus, the term viral pneumonia encompasses a range of imaging findings some of which are not typical for COVID-19.

span.label: features `REPORTED IN THE LITERATURE TO BE FREQUENTLY AND MORE SPECIFICALLY SEEN IN COVID-19 PNEUMONIA IN THE CURRENT PANDEMIC`
span.quote: Typical features are those that are reported in the literature to be frequently and more specifically seen in COVID-19 pneumonia in the current pandemic

span.label: features `REPORTED IN COVID-19 PNEUMONIA BUT NOT SPECIFIC ENOUGH TO ARRIVE AT A RELATIVELY CONFIDENT RADIOLOGIC DIAGNOSIS`
span.quote: Indeterminate features are those that have been reported in COVID-19 pneumonia but are not specific enough to arrive at a relatively confident radiologic diagnosis. An example would be diffuse GGO without a clear distribution ( Figs 5 , 6 ). This finding is common in COVID-19 pneumonia but occurs in a wide variety of diseases such as acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Pneumocystis infection, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, which are difficult to distinguish by imaging alone.

span.label: features `UNCOMMON OR NOT OCCURRING IN COVID-19 pneumonia AND MORE TYPICAL OF OTHER DISEASES`
span.quote: Atypical features are those that are reported to be uncommon or not occurring in COVID-19 pneumonia and are more typical of other diseases such as lobar or segmental consolidation in the setting of a bacterial pneumonia, cavitation from necrotizing pneumonia, and tree-in-bud opacities with centrilobular nodules, as can occur with a variety of community acquired infections and aspiration

span.label: `NO PARENCHYMAL ABNORMALITIES THAT COULD BE ATTRIBUTABLE TO INFECTION. Specifically, GGO AND CONSOLIDATION ARE ABSENT`
span.quote: Negative for pneumonia implies that there are no parenchymal abnormalities that could be attributable to infection. Specifically, GGO and consolidation are absent. Importantly, there may be no findings on CT early in COVID-19.

span.label: 60-98 — the reported range for chest CT in COVID-19, attributed by the authors to the lack of strict diagnostic criteria for imaging
span.quote: The reported sensitivities and specificities of CT for COVID-19 vary widely (60%–98% and 25%–53%, respectively) ( 26 – 29 ), likely due to the retrospective nature of the currently published studies, including lack of strict diagnostic criteria for imaging and procedural differences for confirming infection.

span.label: 25-53 — the matching specificity range for the same instrument
span.quote: The reported sensitivities and specificities of CT for COVID-19 vary widely (60%–98% and 25%–53%, respectively) ( 26 – 29 ), likely due to the retrospective nature of the currently published studies, including lack of strict diagnostic criteria for imaging and procedural differences for confirming infection.

span.label: 42-71 — the reported range for RT-PCR - the reference standard the imaging is scored against
span.quote: Early reports of RT-PCR sensitivity vary considerably, ranging from 42% to 71% ( 26 , 27 ), and an initially negative RT-PCR may take up to 4 days to convert in a patient with COVID-19

span.label: 11 — the number approved for use in China between 26 January and 12 March 2020, with varying levels of sensitivity
span.quote: Eleven different RT-PCR tests were approved for use in China between January 26 and March 12, 2020, with varying levels of sensitivity.

span.label: 20 — the share of COVID-19 patients who may have coexistent infections, complicating which of the four categories an image belongs to
span.quote: We anticipate cases with mixed imaging findings, that is, those that have both typical and atypical imaging features for COVID-19. Recent analysis suggests that over 20% of patients with COVID-19 may have coexistent infections complicating the categorization of imaging observations ( 35 ). The radiologist will have to determine whether or not these findings are part of the same process or are unrelated.

span.label: the term recommended in place of COVID-19 for incidental findings, chosen for what it avoids rather than for what it says
span.quote: It should be noted that viral pneumonias have a wide variety of imaging manifestations, some of which are atypical or less common in COVID-19 such as tree-in-bud opacities and other small nodules, bronchial wall thickening, and bronchial mucus plugs ( 12 ). Thus, the term viral pneumonia encompasses a range of imaging findings some of which are not typical for COVID-19.
